lessons.title: Reading Where We Are in the Current Cycle: Signals to Watch

children.text: A Checklist You Can Run Whenever You're Asking the Question

This lesson will not tell you where the oil, gold and metals cycles stand today, and deliberately so. A specific call made now would be stale within months, while the diagnostic checklist behind that call stays useful for years. What follows pulls together the indicators scattered across every earlier chapter into one reference you can actually run, whenever you happen to be reading this, to form your own view.

body.text: The point of this framework isn't to tell you where the cycle is today. It's to give you the checklist, so you can answer that question yourself, whenever you're the one asking it.

children.text: Two Terms Worth Defining Precisely, Since They Keep Coming Up

markDefs.definition: A futures market condition where futures prices are higher than the current spot price, typically reflecting storage costs and ample near-term supply.
A futures market condition where futures prices are lower than the current spot price, typically reflecting near-term supply tightness.

children.text: You've seen storage and roll costs referenced a few times already. The formal terms are worth locking in now.
is when futures prices sit above the spot price, usually signalling ample supply.

is the reverse, futures below spot, usually signalling near-term tightness. As a rule of thumb, persistent backwardation leans bullish for near-term prices and persistent contango leans bearish, though both also reflect storage economics as much as pure sentiment.

A falling rig count after a price slump signals shale pulling back; strong OPEC+ compliance signals discipline is holding

body.text: No single row in this table is decisive on its own. A falling rig count with weak demand data can still mean lower prices ahead. Extreme speculative positioning in gold can stay extreme for longer than seems reasonable. Treat this as a checklist to build a rounded view, not a set of individually sufficient signals.

body.title: Before You Take a View on Any Commodity Cycle
steps: Identify which of the four phases from Chapter 1 the commodity looks closest to right now: oversupply/trough, stabilisation, demand catching supply, or boom/peak
Check recent capex and drilling or mining investment trends, since Chapter 1's supply lag means today's investment decisions are tomorrow's supply
Check the relevant inventory signal: the futures curve shape for oil, or exchange warehouse stock levels for metals
Check the commodity-specific driver covered in its chapter: real rates and the dollar for gold, OPEC+ and shale for oil, China data for metals
Ask whether a longer supercycle-level force, like the energy transition debate from the previous lesson, could be overriding the ordinary cyclical signal
Check whether speculative positioning looks stretched in one direction, which can be a useful contrarian flag even when the fundamental signals look clear

points: This framework is deliberately built to stay useful over time: a specific call on where the cycle stands goes stale quickly, but the checklist for making that call does not.

Contango and backwardation, futures pricing above or below spot, are the formal terms for the storage and inventory signals referenced throughout this course, and both carry real information about near-term supply tightness.

Oil, gold and metals each have their own dashboard: rig counts and the futures curve for oil, real yields and central bank buying for gold, and China's PMI and credit data alongside LME inventories for metals.
No single signal is decisive by itself. Build a rounded view across the checklist, and stay alert to a supercycle-level force potentially overriding the ordinary cyclical read.
The final lesson turns this diagnostic checklist into an actual portfolio positioning framework across all three commodities.
